title: Explicit Reasoning Makes Better Judges: A Systematic Study on Accuracy, Efficiency, and Robustness

bias_targets.methodology: Flipping the presentation order of the candidate responses and evaluating the consistency of the model's judgments.
Inserting a prompt statement claiming that a majority of people (e.g., '90% of people') prefer one of the assistants to test conformity influence.
Injecting a sentence that links a response to a well-known system name or authority (e.g., 'Qwen3', 'ChatGPT', or 'Human Expert') rather than an anonymized label.
Adding a sentence to the prompt specifying the assistant's identity in terms of sensitive demographic categories, such as gender, race, or health status (e.g., 'Female/Refugee').

Appending irrelevant but positive secondary details to a response (e.g., stating the assistant volunteers at an animal shelter) to see if it distracts the judge from evaluating the main quality of the answer.
Using a teacher model to artificially increase the length of a rejected response with semantically redundant sentences to test if the judge inherently prefers longer answers.
